en: *The Scripture on the Ten Abodes of Bodhisattvas Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
The Buddha’s exposition on the twelve periods of the bodhisattva precepts was concluded. Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “Bodhi...”
"By what merits does a bodhisattva attain these ten stages?
I pray that the God among Gods will explain this in detail.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent! Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!
You have shown great concern for others and brought great peace and security to many.”
"I shall explain its essentials for you in detail; listen attentively and receive it with heedfulness.
Mañjuśrī replied, "I accept your instruction."
The Buddha said:
"There are the merits of the bodhisattvas of the ten abodes, each of which has its own degrees of superiority and inferiority, and they follow their own sequential order. Mañjuśrī said:
“What are the ten? “First, dwelling in the bodhisattva-dharma-abode of *pāraṃgati*.
The Buddha said:

“From the very beginning, he saw that the Buddha was of incomparable and exquisite countenance; gazing upon his facial features, one could never tire of them, nor could anyone ever surpass him. He was noble and honorable beyond all measure, and there was no one who could excel in his teachings.”
Seeing that the Buddha’s majestic power and ritual conduct were thus, they gradually entered the path of the Buddha.
He further opened the way for them and guided them, teaching and delivering them all according to their inclinations; seeing their toil and suffering, he felt deep compassion for them.
Gradually understanding the Buddha’s words, they placed their faith and inclination in them.
Newly initiating the resolve to study the Buddha-way, they desired to fully comprehend the ten difficult points of the Buddha’s wisdom and sought to attain them all.
“What are the ten difficult-to-attain states? They are the ten powers of a Buddha.

First, one shall make offerings to the Buddha; second, one shall instruct others according to their inclinations; third, one shall be born into positions of honor and nobility in every place of rebirth; fourth, there shall be none in the heavens above or the world below who can equal one; fifth, one shall fully attain the wisdom of a Buddha; sixth, in every life and place of rebirth, one shall behold immeasurable Buddhas.”

Seventh, they have fully attained all the Buddha’s sutras; eighth, they have completely transcended all birth and death; ninth, they will soon be liberated from this world; tenth, they shall deliver and liberate all people throughout the ten directions.
"2. What is the dwelling in the dharma of an Aśubha Bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:
"There are ten ways of attending to the people of the ten directions."

What are the ten mentalities? First, to mindfully contemplate all that is good in the world; second, a pure mind; third, a mind of universal peace and security; fourth, a supple and gentle mind; fifth, a mind of universal impartial love; sixth, a mind that intends only to bestow gifts upon others; seventh, a mind that always maintains equal protection toward all; eighth, to mindfully regard others as no different from one's own body; ninth, a mind that regards the people of the ten directions as one would regard a teacher; and tenth, a mind that regards the people of the ten directions as one would regard a Buddha.
"Ajita, a bodhisattva’s Dharma requires that they study many sūtras;
having studied many sūtras, they should dwell in solitary retreat;
having dwelt in solitary retreat, they should always attend upon a virtuous teacher and be easy to direct while in the presence of that virtuous teacher."
At all times, one should act with vigor according to the occasion;
having acted with vigor, one should study human wisdom.
In the interim, one should fully retain the teachings received and never forget them.
Since they do not forget [this], they should dwell in a state of peace and security. Why is this?
Because it brings benefit to the people of the ten directions.
"Third, what is the dwelling of the Bodhisattva who dwells in the Dharma, which is likened to space?
The Buddha said:
"One enters into all dharmas by means of ten matters."

What are the ten matters? First, that all things are impermanent; second, that all things are characterized by suffering; third, that all things are empty; fourth, that all things are not mine; fifth, that all things have no abiding place; sixth, that all things provide no benefit; seventh, that all things have no cessation; eighth, that all things have no location; ninth, that all things are without attachment; and tenth, that everything is non-existent.
That all phenomena enter into a single phenomenon, and that a single phenomenon enters into all phenomena—this is the teaching of the Bodhisattva A-cha (Aja).
Fourth, what is the dwelling of the Bodhisattva Dharma-dwelling in the stage of Jamaki?
The Buddha said:
"There are ten matters by which one always aspires to be born in the presence of a Buddha."

First, not returning again; second, reflecting deeply upon the Buddha; third, reflecting deeply upon the Dharma; fourth, with a mind focused on the Sangha of bhikṣus, regarding all people of the ten directions with a heart of loving-kindness; fifth, contemplating that all phenomena are non-existent; sixth, that the buddha-fields of the ten directions are all empty space; seventh, that what was accomplished in past lives is utterly non-existent; eighth, that all things are like illusions and are all empty space; ninth, that all diligent efforts and sufferings are non-existent; tenth, that nirvāṇa is empty space and likewise non-existent.
For this reason, one is born within the Buddha-dharma; this is the teaching of the Bodhisattva Śamāgri.
Fifth, what is the dwelling of the Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna? It is the dwelling in the Dharma. What is meant by this?
The Buddha said:
“All the meritorious deeds performed deliver the people of the ten directions.
There are ten matters.”

First, to protect all people of the ten directions; second, to mindfully contemplate the goodness of all people of the ten directions; third, to mindfully contemplate all people of the ten directions so as to bring them peace and security; fourth, to love all people of the ten directions; fifth, to compassionately mindfully regard all people of the ten directions; sixth, to mindfully contemplate all people of the ten directions so that they do not commit evil; seventh, to lead all people of the ten directions into the path of the bodhisattvas; eighth, to purify all people of the ten directions; ninth, to deliver and liberate all people of the ten directions; tenth, to cause all people of the ten directions to enter parinirvāṇa.
This is the *pāyusambhava* bodhisattva-dharma teaching.
"Sixth, what is the *ajitasambhava* bodhisattva-dharma abiding?
The Buddha said:
“There are ten dharmas of profound compassion and loving-kindness.
First, when someone speaks of the Buddha’s virtues or faults, one’s mind remains unchanged;
second, when one speaks of the Dharma’s virtues or faults, one’s mind remains unchanged.”
Third, when speaking of the good and evil of bodhisattvas, his mind remains without variation;
fourth, when seeking those on the path of bodhisattvas who mutually guide one another regarding good and evil, his mind remains without variation;
fifth, when someone says that the people of the ten directions are more or fewer in number, his mind remains without variation.
Sixth, when observing people throughout the ten directions who lead one another toward good or evil, his mind remains without differentiation;
seventh, when someone among them says that people in the ten directions are easy or difficult to liberate, his mind remains without differentiation;
eighth, if someone speaks of the extent of the Dharma—whether it be much or little—his mind remains without differentiation.
Ninth, there are those who preach the Dharma with minds that do not differ whether they are subject to destruction or indestructible;
tenth, there are those whose minds do not differ regarding the existence or non-existence of dharmas.
This is the teaching for the *agrasambodhi* bodhisattva.
"Seventh, what is the dwelling of the *avaivartika* bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:
“There are ten matters in which a bodhisattva remains firm and unshakable.
First, whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, his mind does not waver or retreat.
Second, whether there is the Dharma or no Dharma, he does not waver or retreat.”
Third, there is the non-retrogression of the presence or absence of bodhisattvas;
fourth, the non-retrogression of the seeking or non-seeking of the bodhisattva path;
fifth, the non-retrogression of attaining or not attaining through the upholding of this Dharma.
Sixth, whether there are Buddhas of the past or no Buddhas of the past, he does not waver or turn back;
seventh, whether there will be Buddhas of the future or no Buddhas of the future, he does not waver or turn back;
eighth, whether there are Buddhas of the present or no Buddhas of the present, he does not waver or turn back.
Ninth, when the Buddha’s wisdom is exhausted or inexhaustible, he remains unmoved and does not regress;
tenth, regarding the manifold or singular aspects of the affairs of the future, past, and present worlds, he remains unmoved and does not regress.
This is the teaching for an avaivartika bodhisattva.
"Eighth: What is the dharma-abiding of the *kumārabhūta* (youthful) bodhisattva? It is as follows:"
The Buddha said: “A bodhisattva abides in ten matters. First, his bodily actions, verbal expressions, and mental thoughts are all pure and clean.

Second, there is no one who can find fault with him. Third, he can, with a single thought, determine in which place he wishes to be reborn. Fourth, he knows who among the people of the ten directions possesses a compassionate heart. Fifth, he fully knows what is trusted and relied upon throughout the ten directions. Sixth, he fully knows the various kinds of people throughout the ten directions. Seventh, he fully knows the deeds performed by the people of the ten directions. Eighth, he fully knows the formation and destruction of all buddha-fields in the ten directions. Ninth, having attained the power of spiritual feet (ṛddhipāda), he can fly wherever he intends to go. Tenth, all dharmas are entirely pure and clean.”
This is the teaching for the Kumārabhūta bodhisattva, the youthful male.
"Ninth, what is the dwelling of the bodhisattva's dharma-dwelling as a Yuvarāja?
The Buddha said:
"It is obtained through ten matters."

First, he fully knows the origins from which the people of the ten directions are born; second, he fully knows the bonds of affection and love to which the people of the ten directions are tied; third, he fully knows the thoughts of the people of the ten directions, including their beginnings, ends, and whence they come; fourth, he fully knows the past lives and future destinies of the people of the ten directions; fifth, he fully knows the various kinds of dharmas of the people of the ten directions; sixth, he fully knows the various kinds of transformations contemplated by the people of the ten directions; seventh, he fully knows the virtues, evils, and destructions of all Buddha-fields; eighth, he fully knows the infinite matters of the past, future, and present; ninth, he fully knows the similarities and differences among the people of the ten directions; tenth, he fully knows how to teach the people of the ten directions by preaching the Dharma of emptiness.
This is the teaching of the Bodhisattva Yuraśa. [Question:
"Tenth, what is the dwelling of the Bodhisattva of the Unexcelled State (A-vyaya)?
The Buddha said:
"When a Bodhisattva enters into the ten knowledges, they are able to discern and understand ten matters.
First, by what cause should one cause the Buddha-fields of the ten directions to tremble?"
Second, I shall clearly understand the affairs within incalculable Buddha-fields;
third, I shall daily appoint bodhisattvas to those incalculable Buddha-fields;
fourth, I shall daily deliver and liberate the sentient beings within those incalculable Buddha-fields.
Fifth, I shall bring peace and security to sentient beings within countless Buddha-fields;
sixth, there shall be no one throughout the ten directions who does not hear my voice and, filled with joy, attain liberation;
seventh, I shall cause all people throughout the ten directions to realize the Buddha-way and all to leave their homes to become śramaṇas.
Eighth, I fully know the thoughts of good and evil entertained by people throughout the ten directions;
ninth, I shall cause all people throughout the ten directions to be inwardly established within the Buddha-way, causing them all to resolve upon the mind of a bodhisattva;
tenth, I shall deliver and liberate all people throughout the ten directions.

“Āyuṣmān Ajita, a bodhisattva is utterly unable to comprehend the conduct of the body, the speech of the mouth, the thoughts of the mind, or the deeds performed by an *anupamacaryā* (A-yi-yen) bodhisattva; they are utterly unable to comprehend the affairs of an *anupamacaryā* bodhisattva.
They cannot know their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), nor can they know their flight;
nor can they ever fathom the past, future, or present affairs of an *anupamacaryā* bodhisattva—this is the teaching of the *anupamacaryā* bodhisattva.”

When the Buddha had spoken these words, seventy-two thousand beings, including the Bodhisattva Saṃtuṣita, were all greatly elated and filled with joy; each manifested a radiance that shone forth, illuminating one another in succession.
Each adjusted their robes with propriety, prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground before the Buddha to pay him homage, and then departed.
Thus ends the *Buddhabhāṣita-bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
